newsitem.title: UK: LME aluminium/zinc stocks fall in week, copper up.
newsitem.headline: LME aluminium/zinc stocks fall in week, copper up.

text.p: London Metal Exchange (LME) aluminium stocks kept falling relentlessly this week and futures prices at long last reacted, though scepticism over how much material was going to consumers continued to reverberate around the market.

Elsewhere, copper inventories soared amid the traditionally slow summer period while zinc stocks fell, though again traders and analysts pondered to what extent consumer demand was helping to erode stock levels.

Aluminium inventories in official LME warehouses fell this week by 17,800 tonnes to 636,575 tonnes after dropping by a similar amount last week. Since the beginning of the year, stocks have declined by 298,500 or 31.9 percent.
Despite scepticism by some quarters three months delivery prices finally reacted to the falls driving above resistance levels to trade around $1,600 a tonne.
Some in the market said that a large majority of the stock was going to consumers despite the summer lull, while others said it was going into consignment stocks.
"While stocks on the LME are ample, a large proportion of these are believed to be in strong hands of financing deals," brokers GNI said in their daily report.
"Therefore such a move (three month) is not expected," GNI added.
Copper stocks gained by 29,075 tonnes. Total stocks now stand at 210,225 tonnes up 94,550 or 81.7 percent since the beginning of the year.

The move above the psychological level of 200,000 tonnes sent the market to a low of $2,272 earlier this week. Traders said the recent wide backwardation had attracted metal in to LME warehouses. On Friday copper's cash to three months was indicated at $50, against $270 early last week.
"The spreads continue to contract as increased lending and physical deliveries add to the market's woes," GNI said.
Copper stocks are expected to rise next week as further Chinese, Taiwanese and Korean metal are delivered into LME warehouses.
"Demand for copper is seasonally slow expect stocks to rise," Angus MacMillan of LME brokers Billiton said.

Zinc inventories fell by 15,000 tonnes to 400,300 tonnes a fall of 100,575 tonnes or 20.1 percent this year. The tumbling stocks impacted on the futures market which prompted three months delivery to soar to a seven-year high of $1,600.
Traders said that fundamentally zinc remained sound.
They also noted news of potentially large losses of a Chinese zinc producer which must cover its short position.
Several traders believe that zinc stocks will continue to fall.
But again questions were asked on where the stock was going. "The fundamentals are good but not that good to justify the fall in stocks," MacMillan of Billiton said.
Others agreed saying that a major European merchant was taking metal off warrant which was believed not to be directly heading to consumption.
"The market is running far ahead of its fundamentals," an analyst said.
Lead stocks built by 2,675 tonnes during the week, but were down 175 tonnes on the year. Traders said although stocks are rising the pace of the increases was slow considering the time of year.
They expected lead inventories to fall near-term as automobile battery producers restock.
